title: Strengthening Structures
summary: How triangulation, struts and ties, folding, tubes, arches, beams and good foundations make structures strong, stable and rigid, and the properties of materials used.

items: **Strength**: the ability to carry a load without breaking.
**Stability**: the ability to stay upright and not fall over. A **low centre of gravity** and a **wide base** make a structure more stable.
**Rigidity**: the ability to keep its shape without bending, twisting or collapsing.

notes.text: A square frame made of four strips joined at the corners can easily be pushed into a parallelogram. Adding a diagonal member divides it into two **triangles**, and a triangle cannot change shape unless one of its sides breaks or bends. This is called **triangulation**. It is used in roof trusses, cranes, pylons and bridges.

notes.title: Fixing a wobbly frame
notes.problem: A square frame made of four sticks leans over easily when pushed at a corner. How can you stop this using one more stick?
steps: A square can change shape without any stick bending, as its corners act as hinges.
A triangle cannot change shape unless a side breaks.
A diagonal stick divides the square into two triangles.

rows: The diagonal brace under a shelf that pushes up
A wire or cable holding up a pole or a gate

notes.title: Strut or tie?
notes.problem: A shelf bracket has a horizontal top bar fixed to a wall and a diagonal bar below supporting its outer end. A load hangs from the outer end. Which is the strut and which the tie?
steps: The load pulls the top bar away from the wall, stretching it: that is tension.
The diagonal is pushed towards the wall: that is compression.
A member in tension is a tie and one in compression is a strut.
notes.answer: The top bar is a tie and the diagonal is a strut.

rows: Folds make thin sheets much stiffer
Hollow tubes are strong and light
Spread the load outwards and down to the supports; the arch is in compression
Shaped to resist bending with little material
Steel beams in buildings and bridges
Triangular plates at joints make corners stronger
Steel rods (in tension) inside concrete (strong in compression)
Spread the weight into the ground so the structure does not sink or topple

notes.label: Exam tip
notes.text: Concrete is strong in **compression** but weak in **tension**. Steel is strong in **tension**. That is why steel rods are placed in the parts of a concrete beam that are stretched.

items: **Durability** (lasts a long time and resists weather): stainless steel, treated timber, brick.
**Cost** and **availability** are also important when choosing materials.
